client_brief:
Eighteen conference badges with portraits that match and records that do not drift

The Meridian Summit registration desk needs a correct badge for every attending delegate. We have eighteen self-submitted photographs and last year's venue-bureau PDF, but not its working file.

The photographic problem and the record problem are equally important. Please align the portrait framing while keeping individual skin faithful, then bind each person to their own complete registration details, including post-nominals.

Badge run
One page per attending delegate in registration order at true badge trim, rendered at 300 ppi, every field the 2026 badge carried present on every badge and bound verbatim from the registration export including post-nominals, with each delegate's own portrait in the correct graphic frame. Accompanied by one single-badge file per delegate named to that delegate and identity-verified by opening it, plus 300 ppi proofs. Produced by reverse-engineering the bureau's flat PDF into a live merge template, which is handed back with the record of how it was derived and of what it cannot carry.

Portrait set
Eighteen self-submitted portraits of wildly different provenance brought to one house treatment with individual skin held faithful rather than averaged, delivered at a consistent badge framing with the same eye line and head size across the set, plus one licensed venue context frame graded into the same neutral. Every output at or below its source pixel dimensions, with a per-portrait parameter log, one line per portrait on why it differs from its neighbours, and every crop and resize response's reported metadata transcribed.

Preflight evidence
A client-facing preflight package showing representative first, middle, last, longest, and exception records at true output size, with page count, dimensions, overflow, image binding, naming, and record identity checks.

Attached: delegate_headshots/ (18 files, 900 x 1200 to 4200 x 5600); registration_export.csv (21 rows); badge_2026_PRINT.pdf; lectern_plate.jpg (3900 x 2600); tracks_note.txt.

We expect true-size proofs of representative and difficult records, including the longest and exception entries. A successful merge message is not a substitute for checking the exported badges and their individual filenames.

Alongside the finished work, we need a delivery manifest, the editable sources specified above, final exports, a short production and exceptions note and the normalised data and field-mapping record. Keep a clear record of the supplied files used, retained for reference, superseded and rejected. Approved source information remains authoritative. Record omissions, substitutions, reconciliations and quality limits, and do not use an undeclared replacement or invented fact to conceal a source problem.

This is a fixed-price commission at $6,000-$12,000, with a target of 4 to 6 weeks. The agreed review allowance is direction approval, first-production proof, and two consolidated revision rounds. New deliverable classes, new source creation, extra records, and client copy changes after approval are quoted separately.

source_provenance.statement: The scenario is synthesized from the repository's laundered Upwork and Freelancer source anchors. It is not represented as a verbatim live listing.
source_provenance.original_anchor: The batch ledger carries no quoted posting for this slot, so the anchor here is the recurring posted-job shape rather than one quoted advertisement. Primary anchor: the Upwork commission repeatedly listed as 'InDesign data merge for conference name badges, roster CSV plus per-attendee headshots', posted by event organisers who hold last year's badge only as a flat print file from the venue's print bureau, have no working file and nobody who remembers how it was built, and need this year's roster, organisations, tracks and photographs put through the same badge, delivered as one ordered press file for the on-site printer plus individual files for the reprint desk. Co-anchor: the Upwork and Freelancer.com 'event collateral designer, badges plus registration signage plus closing deck' listings, which bundle the badge run with the registration-desk board, the session-room door cards and the closing slides, because organisers buy the room as one job and never the badge alone. Laundered to the fictional Meridian Council and its Meridian Summit; no real company, person, venue, sponsor or trademark appears. The ledger recorded this slot as a badge merge and nothing else, which is one surface and one deliverable class. LAYOUT-23 restores the commission the organisers actually post: eighteen portraits taken by eighteen different people have to be made into one wall before any of them binds, the summit mark has to be recovered because nobody kept the file, and the badge run, the registration board and the closing slides all have to agree with each other in a room where every delegate paid twenty-four hundred dollars to be there.

price_band_and_audience: Twenty-four hundred dollars a seat, eighteen seats, invitation only. Delegates are 40 to 65, they run regional transmission networks, sit on infrastructure funds or write utility policy, and they have been to two hundred conferences. The band is load-bearing. At this tier the correct badge is heavy, quiet and photo-forward: one restrained neutral, generous space, the name set large and calm, the organisation smaller but complete, the track carried as a small typographic distinction rather than a shouted colour block, and the portrait treated like a portrait. Push it toward the bright, playful, colour-blocked, text-only badge that a free two-hundred-person community meetup correctly uses and the delegate reads it as a name sticker, which at this price is an insult they will mention to the person who invited them. Push it the other way into a decorated or celebratory register and it reads as a gala rather than a closed-door working session. A real posted job of this shape runs 1,600 to 3,200 dollars fixed, or 45 to 75 dollars an hour across 30 to 45 hours.

assets_supplied.name: delegate_headshots/ (18 files, 900 x 1200 to 4200 x 5600)
assets_supplied.kind: Self-submitted portraits, one per delegate, collected through the registration form. Studio headshots, crops out of group photographs, and one phone picture taken in a hotel corridor.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Everyone sent their own. Some are proper, some are not. They have to look like they were all taken for us."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Two faults, neither stated. Five portraits sit within a whisker of their own background in value (a light grey jacket on a pale grey sweep, platinum hair against cream, a white shirt against a white wall), so an automatic isolation reports complete success while quietly biting through the shoulder line and the hair edge, and the damage is invisible until the cut sits on the badge's own ground. Four others were cropped out of group photographs and are a fraction of the size of the rest, so a resize to the badge frame interpolates them and says so only inside a tradeoff entry that nothing forces anyone to read.

assets_supplied.name: registration_export.csv (21 rows)
assets_supplied.kind: Export from the registration platform, one row per registration, with columns for salutation, first and last name, post-nominals, organisation, job title, track, ticket type, registration timestamp, refund date and a photograph column.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Straight out of the registration system, in the order people signed up. That is the order the printer wants them in."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Twenty-one rows for eighteen badges. One registration was refunded and is flagged only by a date in a column the client never mentions, one delegate registered twice under two different employers (the second is a former one), and one row is the venue's own audiovisual contractor carrying a comped ticket type. Three organisation names run four times the length of the others, two delegates carry post-nominals the client has said must not be dropped, and the photograph column holds full local paths without the prefix the merge's own image contract requires.

assets_supplied.name: badge_2026_PRINT.pdf
assets_supplied.kind: The venue print bureau's flat press PDF of last year's delegate badge, 4 inches by 3 inches landscape, fonts embedded, produced through a full print engine so it converts cleanly. Carries a name line, an organisation line, a track word, a portrait, the summit mark and a check-in code panel.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "What the bureau printed last year. We do not have the working file and nobody here knows how it was built. Keep it exactly as it is."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Three facts nobody at Meridian could tell you. The name, the organisation and the track word came out of the bureau's system as ONE continuous story with tab characters between them rather than as the three separate blocks the printed badge appears to show, so there is nothing to map field by field. The name sits in a fixed-measure frame that does not spill: a string longer than the measure simply stops rendering at the frame edge, the page still renders, and every tool in the chain still reports success. The check-in code is a flat grey rectangle placed as a graphic, the two graphic frames are distinguishable only by their bounds and their link, and the converted document carries no bleed at all.

assets_supplied.name: lectern_plate.jpg (3900 x 2600)
assets_supplied.kind: Photograph of the engraved brass lectern plate carrying the summit mark, shot at a slight angle under the room's downlights.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The only clean version of our mark that exists anywhere. It is the plate on the lectern."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The mark is engraved into polished brass rather than printed, so it reads as a value shift in a reflective surface rather than as ink, and a prompt naming the plate or the lectern pulls the selection to the whole brass rectangle instead of the engraved line. The wordmark encloses two counters that no one-call knockout can punch open, and the downlights lay a bright specular band diagonally across one word.

assets_supplied.name: tracks_note.txt
assets_supplied.kind: Four lines from the summit producer naming the three delegate tracks and what each is for.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Operators, Capital, Policy. Operators run the network, Capital funds it, Policy regulates it. People want to know who they are standing next to."

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether the isolation held its edge on this particular person. Five of the eighteen delegates sit within a whisker of their own background in value: a light grey jacket on a pale grey sweep, platinum hair against cream, a white shirt against a white wall. On those frames the automatic isolation returns a clean, confident, entirely plausible cut-out and has quietly taken the shoulder line, the collar or the hair edge away with the background, because there was no value difference for it to find. Which portraits behave this way is a property of these specific photographs (this person, wearing this, in front of that) and cannot be read off the roster, the filenames or the source previews. The damage is also invisible against transparency: it appears only once the cut is placed on the badge's own ground, where a missing shoulder reads as a printing fault rather than as a bad cut.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering cannot dodge it and care alone does not either, because the tool reports success either way and the returned cut-out looks correct until it is composited against the ground the badge actually uses. Nothing states it: the brief says the portraits are a mixed bag and asks for one consistent wall, which is an ordinary client requirement, and no asset description names the five delegates at risk. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is to abandon the automatic route for those portraits in favour of an explicit selection of the person, inverted and filled to the chosen ground, and then to re-take the ground decision for the whole set, since a ground that rescues a platinum-haired delegate may bury a dark-suited one.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Re-isolate the affected portraits by selecting the person explicitly, inverting and filling to the ground rather than asking for an automatic knockout, then re-place all eighteen on the ground together and re-decide the ground, because five portraits produced by a different route will not sit with the other thirteen unless the ground choice is re-made across the set. Record the route per delegate in the handover so the reprint desk knows which files were produced how.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A registration wall at a twenty-four-hundred-dollar summit on which five delegates have no left shoulder and one has a hole in her hairline, printed, laminated and hung, with every tool in the chain having reported success.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: That the per-delegate check-in code the client asked for cannot actually be produced on this surface, and that the tools say the opposite at every step. The code mapping is documented, is accepted and normalised by the validator, and the template preparation returns a clean success message. Nothing is created. The round-tripped document shows the code frame keeping its original static link with none of the markers a live code would carry, and a rendered badge shows the same flat grey rectangle it always had. There is no error, no warning and no diagnostic anywhere in the chain, and the printed badge looks finished.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering cannot dodge it, and reading the documentation makes it worse rather than better, because the documentation describes the capability as working and the validator agrees, so a diligent agent has every reason to believe it landed. Nothing states it: the brief asks for a scan code because the desk scans people in, which is an ordinary organiser requirement, and the acceptance bar asks only that anything the badge cannot carry be named before print. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is to drop a requested feature, re-scope it with the client and propose a different route to check-in, which changes what is delivered rather than re-running what was.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Verify by round-tripping the prepared template and reading the code frame directly rather than trusting the success message, confirm the same on a single rendered badge, then remove the dead mapping so it is not carried silently into the run, and raise it with the client before print with a workable alternative: one static event code on every badge with check-in done against the printed delegate number, or per-delegate code artwork produced by the registration platform and bound through the image column exactly as the portraits are. Nothing else in the badge changes, which is precisely why it is easy to leave broken.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Eighteen badges printed and laminated with a grey rectangle where the code should be, discovered by a scanner at seven in the morning at a summit where the first delegate through the door runs a transmission network.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether each delegate's organisation and name actually fit the badge. The name and organisation came out of the bureau's system inside one continuous story sitting in a fixed-measure frame, and a fixed frame in this layout does not spill: a string longer than the measure simply stops rendering at the frame edge. The page renders, the page count is right, the merge reports success, the proof looks composed, and one delegate's employer reads as a plausible shorter name with nothing anywhere to indicate that anything is missing. Which records overflow depends on the measure the conversion happened to produce, which is not a parameter and is not under anyone's control, so it can only be learned by merging the real roster and reading each rendered page at true trim.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering cannot dodge it: the frame's real measure exists only after the conversion, and the truncation exists only after the real strings are bound into it, so no amount of planning reaches it earlier. Nothing states it: the brief says nothing may be shortened or abbreviated, which is the client's standing requirement rather than a warning, and no asset description tells the agent which three organisations are long. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is a scope conversation and a layout decision rather than another merge of the same thing.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Read every rendered badge at true trim against its export row, identify which records are being cut and where, then take the decision the client asked for: raise it in writing before print rather than abbreviating, and propose what is actually available, which is a second badge variant for the long-organisation records merged as a record-range subset, or the organisation carried across a second line, never a shortened string. Re-run only the affected subset and read it at trim again rather than assuming the second attempt took.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Badges handed to three senior delegates on which their employer's name is cut off mid-word, from an organiser whose entire proposition is that this room is worth twenty-four hundred dollars a seat.

decision_gates: The surface split: badges to the merge surface because the layout is fixed client property and the run is one record per page, room set to HTML authoring because it needs three canvas sizes and must stay editable.
Which portraits set the house treatment, knowing a studio headshot and a hotel-corridor phone picture cannot both be the reference.
How far to correct an individual portrait before the correction stops matching the wall and starts changing the person.
The badge crop policy across eighteen faces, decided as a set, and constrained by the four sources that are a fraction of the size of the rest.
The badge ground, chosen against eighteen different jackets, shirts and hair colours rather than against the best-looking single portrait.
Isolation route per delegate: the one-call knockout is right for a dark suit on a mid grey and wrong for a light jacket on a pale sweep, and the wrong route reports success either way.
Whether the mark is selected from the engraved line or from the brass plate it is cut into, which is entirely a matter of how the selection is worded.
Which of two indistinguishable graphic frames holds the portrait rather than the summit mark.

why_not_vlm: Paste this brief and these files into a frontier image model and it returns pictures of badges with invented people on them. IDENTITY: these are eighteen named human beings who will stand at a registration desk wearing their own face, their own employer and their own post-nominals, and a generated portrait is not that person, which at an invitation-only summit is the one failure nobody forgives. SPEC: the client needs one page per attending delegate in registration order at true badge trim and 300 ppi, eighteen separately named badge files each containing the delegate their filename claims, every value bound verbatim from a registration export that contains three rows which must not become badges, and no delivered file larger than its source. None of that can be produced or checked by generation. EDITABILITY: two deliverables are defined by being editable, a live merge template so next year's roster is a data change, and a native document with live text and real vector so the running order can move the week before. And the middle of this engagement is verification against material reality: did this cut-out keep its shoulder, did this placeholder actually get created, does this code panel contain anything at all, does this organisation fit the frame it was bound into. That is not a generation problem.
